title: Rome allows improper 'sin' for concupiscence; little distance from Protestants
source_text: XXXII. Denique quamvis negent concupiscentiam, quae est in regenitis, peccatum vocari debere, secundum veram & propriam hujus vocis acceptionem, agnoscunt tamen illam dici posse iniquitatem & peccatum largiori, & improprio quodam sensu: quatenus scilicet, ex peccato orta est, & ad peccatum ducit: imo in seipsa habet quandam inordinationem, quatenus, scilicet, per eam facultates inferiores quae, secundum ordinem a Deo primitus institutum, parere debent superioribus, illis inobedientes & refractariae redduntur. Adeoque in hunc sensum interpretantur plura Apostoli loca in epist. ad Rom. ubi concupiscentiam peccati nomine designat; ut videre est apud eundem Bellarminum, lib. 5. de Amissione gratiae, & statu peccati, cap. 13. Ex quibus omnibus prudenti cuivis colligendum relinquo, quam parum absint ipsi Scholae Romanae Doctores a Protestantium in hoc Articulo doctrina, in quam tamen tam odiose declamant, & tam acerbe invehuntur.
pass_a_gloss: Finally, although they deny that the concupiscence which is in the regenerate ought to be called sin according to the true and proper acceptation of this word, yet they acknowledge that it can be called iniquity and sin in a broader and certain improper sense: inasmuch as it arose from sin and leads to sin; indeed in itself it has a certain inordination, inasmuch as through it the lower faculties which, according to the order first instituted by God, ought to obey the higher, are rendered disobedient and refractory to them. And so in this sense they interpret several places of the Apostle in the epistle to the Romans where he designates concupiscence by the name of sin; as may be seen in the same Bellarmine, book 5 On the Loss of Grace and the State of Sin, chapter 13. From all which I leave it to any prudent person to gather how little the Doctors of the Roman School themselves are distant from the Protestants' doctrine in this Article, against which nevertheless they declaim so hatefully and inveigh so bitterly.
pass_b_english: Rome denies proper 'sin' for regenerate concupiscence yet allows broader/improper sin-language (from sin, to sin, disordered lower powers).
That reading covers Paul's Romans usage (Bellarmine)—so Rome stands little off from Protestants while still railing bitterly.

lemmas.gloss: in a broader and improper sense
